title: The Power Bench
summary: Find AC power and power factor, correct a lagging load, and see why transformers cut line losses.
subject: physics
ncertRef: Section 7.7, Power in an AC circuit, the power factor
learningOutcome: The student can find the average power and wattless current of an AC circuit, correct a power factor with a capacitor, and use a transformer and high voltage to cut the loss in a transmission line.

levels.title: Power and phase
levels.adds: Baseline: P = V I cos φ, with I sin φ the wattless component (Section 7.7).
hints: The component of I along V delivers the power.
The wattless component is I sin φ.

levels.title: Power in a circuit
levels.adds: New idea: in a series LCR circuit only R dissipates power, so P = I²R and cos φ = R/Z (Example 7.8).
hints: Find Z, then the rms current from the peak voltage.

levels.title: Correct the power factor
levels.adds: More steps: a parallel capacitor supplies the wattless current, so the supply current falls (Example 7.7).
hints: The wattless current of the load is V X_L/Z².
The capacitor current is ωCV and leads by 90°.
What remains is the power component, V R/Z².

levels.title: The transformer
levels.adds: New idea: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p and, with no loss, I_p V_p = I_s V_s (Section 7.8).
hints: The voltages are in the ratio of the turns.
An ideal transformer takes in as much power as it delivers.
More turns on the secondary means a higher voltage and a lower current.

levels.title: Power lines
levels.adds: Apply it: stepping the voltage up by k cuts the line current by k and the loss by k² (Example 7.7).
hints: Divide the current by k and square.

misconceptions: The power in an AC circuit is always V I
A transformer increases power as well as voltage
Power is sent at high voltage to make the current larger
